trace.code: Authenticate(ctx) pulls app/token from incoming gRPC metadata, then returns a.validate(app, token)
validate(): expect, err := a.cache.Take(app, func() { return a.store.Hget(a.key, app) })  // Redis hash lookup of the app -> expected token
if err != nil { if a.strict { return Internal } return nil }  // FAIL-OPEN: unknown app (redis.Nil) or ANY Redis error => nil => AUTHENTICATED when strict=false
if token != expect { return Unauthenticated, accessDenied }  // token is only checked when the app resolves; an unknown app never reaches this
UnaryAuthorizeInterceptor calls Authenticator.Authenticate(ctx) and only invokes the handler when it returns nil — so a fail-open nil directly executes the RPC
removed the strict branch and the `return nil` fallback entirely: any lookup error now returns status.Error(codes.Unauthenticated, accessDenied) — fail closed, and StrictControl is deprecated

preconditions: A go-zero zrpc server with Auth enabled in its RpcServerConf (the operator opts into authentication to protect the service)

StrictControl left at its default (false) — the documented JSON `optional` bool zero value. With strict=false any Redis lookup error returns nil (authenticated); strict=true would instead return an Internal error (fail closed, though it leaks internal Redis error details to the client). The default is the vulnerable path.
The attacker can reach the zrpc endpoint over the network and knows (or guesses) any method name; the app name is arbitrary and NOT registered in Redis
No valid credential is required: an unregistered app name makes Hget return redis.Nil, which the default strict=false path treats as success

evidence.vulnerable_version: go-zero <= v1.9.4 (latest release at 2026-11-12; the fix is unreleased on master)
evidence.fixed_version: unreleased (master @ f56630376, 2026-11-01, PR #5848 'fix(security): zrpc Authenticator fails open')
evidence.observed_result: Driving the REAL go-zero v1.9.4 internal/auth.Authenticator against a faithful RESP Redis: a valid (registered) app+token is GRANTED; a wrong token for a registered app is DENIED (Unauthenticated) — proving the authenticator does enforce tokens. An UNKNOWN app ('attacker' with any token) is GRANTED (fail-open), and an injected Redis outage also GRANTs an unregistered caller (total fail-open). Marker printed: RESULT: AUTH BYPASS CONFIRMED.

real_exploit.target: github.com/zeromicro/go-zero v1.9.4 (real checkout at tag f29c8612e86fca4ac1c6b718fd83f73fbe7235eb) — the actual zrpc/internal/auth package is compiled from the real source and its Authenticate() method (the exact call the real UnaryAuthorizeInterceptor makes per request) is driven directly
real_exploit.backend: miniredis v2.35.0 (the faithful in-process Redis speaking the real RESP protocol over a TCP socket — the same backend used by go-zero's own auth regression tests, TestAuthenticatorFailClosed)
real_exploit.demonstrated: The real Authenticator.Authenticate() grants access (returns nil) for an UNKNOWN app name and for a Redis-outage error, while still DENYING a wrong token for a registered app. The fail-open nil is what the real UnaryAuthorizeInterceptor treats as authenticated and passes straight to the RPC handler, so an unauthenticated caller invokes any protected method.
